mainEntity.name: What if my payment doesn't cover the interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your monthly payment is lower than the interest accruing each month, the balance will never be paid off — you'll need to increase the payment above that threshold. The calculator flags any debt whose minimum doesn't cover its interest.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off high-interest debt before investing?

acceptedAnswer.text: As a general rule, paying off debt with a higher interest rate than your expected investment return tends to provide a better guaranteed outcome, though individual circumstances vary.

mainEntity.name: Which is better: avalanche or snowball payoff method?

acceptedAnswer.text: Avalanche (highest interest rate first) saves more money mathematically. Snowball (smallest balance first) can be more motivating since it produces quick wins, even at a slightly higher total cost — the best method is the one you'll actually stick with.

mainEntity.name: Should I pay off debt or save simultaneously?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most financial guidance suggests keeping a small emergency fund while aggressively paying down high-interest debt, then shifting focus to savings once high-interest balances are cleared.

mainEntity.name: How much does avalanche actually save over snowball, in real numbers?

acceptedAnswer.text: On $14,700 across three debts (24.99%, 19.99%, and 11.5% APR) with $300/month extra, avalanche saves $178 in interest over 25 months — but takes until month 12 to eliminate its first debt, versus month 7 for snowball. See the full worked example.

mainEntity.name: Is a 0% balance transfer worth the fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: On a $6,700 balance at 23% APR paid off over 18 months, a 0% intro card with a 3% transfer fee ($201) saves about $1,084 versus staying put. The transfer stops being worth it once your original APR drops below roughly 3.8%.
